lesson.title: The Five-Step Method for Solving Any Related Rates Problem
lesson.summary: Every related rates problem, no matter how different the story sounds, can be solved with the same five-step routine: name the variables, draw the picture, write an equation, differentiate with respect to time, then substitute numbers and solve.
lesson.body:
Related rates word problems can feel unpredictable because the stories are so different: a ladder sliding down a wall, a balloon inflating, a shadow stretching across a parking lot. But underneath the story, every one of these problems is solved with the same fixed procedure, and learning that procedure once is far more useful than trying to memorize each story separately.

The five steps are as follows. First, identify every quantity in the problem that changes over time and give each one a variable name, reserving actual numbers only for quantities that stay constant throughout the whole scenario. Second, draw a diagram of the situation at a generic moment in time and label it with those variable names. Third, write down an equation that relates the variables, drawn from geometry (the Pythagorean theorem, a volume or area formula, similar triangles, a trig ratio), and make sure this equation is true at every instant, not just the one instant the question asks about. Fourth, differentiate both sides of that equation with respect to time t, using implicit differentiation, which turns each variable into a rate term through the chain rule. Fifth, substitute the specific numeric values that describe the instant in question, and solve algebraically for whichever rate is unknown.

The order of steps four and five is not negotiable, and it is the single most common place students lose points. If you substitute a specific numeric value for a changing variable before you differentiate, you have frozen that variable at one instant, and its derivative silently becomes zero, wiping out a term that should have contributed to the answer. The equation from step three has to be treated as a general statement, true for a whole interval of time, right up until the moment you differentiate it. Only after differentiating are you allowed to zoom in on the one instant you actually care about.

Here is the method applied to a clean example. The edge length of a cube is growing at 2 centimeters per second. How fast is its volume growing at the moment the edge length is 4 centimeters? Step one: let s be the edge length and V be the volume, both functions of time; the rate ds/dt = 2 is given and dV/dt at s = 4 is what we want. Step two, in this simple case the diagram is just a cube labeled with side s. Step three: the volume of a cube is V = s^3, true for every value of s the cube ever takes. Step four: differentiate with respect to t, using the power rule together with the chain rule, dV/dt = 3 s^2 (ds/dt). Step five: substitute s = 4 and ds/dt = 2, giving dV/dt = 3(16)(2) = 96 cubic centimeters per second.

With this five-step skeleton in place, the rest of the related rates material is really about getting good at steps one through three for specific kinds of scenarios. Sorting out which symbols are rates and which are instantaneous values, coming next, sharpens step one. Drawing the picture correctly, right after that, sharpens step two. And the five classic problem types that follow, the ladder, the balloon, the shadow, the conical tank, and two cars separating, are really just five different versions of step three, five different geometric relationships to differentiate using exactly this same procedure.
